one_liner: O(N) fountain (rateless) erasure code in C; the author's GF256 build encoded about 6.6x and decoded about 7.9x faster than his CM256 Reed-Solomon at k=m=128.
what_it_does: Turns a message of N = ceil(bytes / block_bytes) blocks (2 to 64,000) into an unbounded stream of packets: IDs below N are the original blocks, higher IDs are repair blocks, and any roughly N + 0.02 received packets recover the message. The legacy C API is wirehair_encoder_create / wirehair_encode / wirehair_decoder_create / wirehair_decode / wirehair_recover (plus wirehair_recover_block for one missing block); a newer V2 API (wirehair_v2_*, with a C++ RAII wirehair.hpp) emits a 32-byte serialized profile descriptor the decoder is built from. It is not a drop-in for a Reed-Solomon API such as CM256's: there is no fixed recovery count, and packets are addressed by ID rather than by erasure position.
how_it_is_fast: It is a hybrid LDPC / Raptor-style code: a sparse binary peeling matrix solved by an O(N) peeling decoder, a Shuffle-2 dense binary submatrix plus a 6x18 GF(256) 'heavy' submatrix to repair what peeling misses, and Gaussian elimination only on the small (about sqrt(N)) residual square matrix, followed by back-substitution (WirehairCodec.h overview). Most row operations are XORs of whole blocks; GF(256) multiply-add uses the bundled gf256 library with SSSE3 shuffles and runtime-gated AVX2, AVX-512 and GFNI paths on x86 and NEON on ARM. Per-N seeds and dense counts are precomputed offline so the matrix for every N is known to be solvable, which keeps cost roughly linear in N instead of the O(K*M) of Cauchy Reed-Solomon.
when_to_use: Large block counts (hundreds to 64,000 blocks; the header says N around 1000 is most efficient) where O(K*M) Reed-Solomon such as CM256 or Longhair is too slow or capped at 255 or 256 total pieces.

Rateless delivery: multicast or broadcast file transfer, satellite or radio links, and store-and-forward relays (wirehair_decoder_becomes_encoder) where the sender cannot know the loss rate in advance.
Heavy-loss or code-rate-1/2 workloads, where its decode time stays flat with the number of losses while matrix Reed-Solomon decode grows with the erasure count.
Projects that need a dependency-free C API with Python bindings, an exported CMake package and a versioned shared-library ABI.
when_not_to_use: Storage or RAID-style layouts that need an MDS guarantee: any N of N + M pieces must decode. Wirehair sometimes needs N + 1 or N + 2 packets (the README's average is N + 0.02; the large-K sweep shows 98.3 to 99.6 percent exact-N success at 10 percent loss).
Small N (below about 128): the README itself calls it a pretty inefficient codec there compared with Fecal (catid/fecal), and N = 1 is rejected.

Few losses on moderate N: the Fecal README measures FEC-AL encoding about 2x faster with about 100 losses at N = 1000, and 4x faster encode and 2x faster decode with about 30 losses, because Wirehair pays a full matrix solve on both sides regardless of how many repair blocks are used.
Pure encode throughput at k = m = 128: the author's own Leopard-RS (an MDS FFT Reed-Solomon) encoded about 3x faster (1965 MB/s vs 662 MB/s) in the same table; Wirehair only won decode there.

Adversarial channels: issue #16 raises that an attacker who knows the deterministic PRNG could choose erasures that make decoding fail well beyond N packets (RaptorQ has the same exposure), and recovered data is not authenticated.

integration.form: static lib (default CMake build; BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON or WIREHAIR_BUILD_BOTH=ON for shared), also usable as a source drop of the gf256 and Wirehair files
integration.dependencies: none external; the C++ runtime and threads library are private link dependencies (pkg-config --static adds them)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (cxx_std_11), CMake 3.15; C consumers use the C header
integration.platforms: x86/x86-64 with SSSE3 base and runtime-dispatched AVX2, AVX-512 and GFNI; ARM with NEON (Apple arm64 included); portable fallback; big-endian supported by the current named profiles (s390x emulation tests). ARM64 Windows support is an open issue (#31). MARCH_NATIVE=ON builds are host-specific.
integration.thread_safety: wirehair_init() is thread-safe; codec objects are not: use one codec per thread or your own lock, and do not race wirehair_encoder_detach_input() with encoding (README).

gotchas: Packet equations are a wire contract separate from the C ABI: the unframed legacy APIs are pinned to the 2026-07 seed-fixup profile (768 peel and 163 dense exact-N seed overrides), so packets made by a pre-fixup build can silently decode to the wrong bytes with a current build; the profile ID cannot be detected from raw packets, so carry it in trusted framing and use the explicit profile APIs.

Decode success only means the equations were solvable: corrupted, mismatched-profile or adversarial packets can 'recover' wrong data, so verify a trusted digest or MAC after wirehair_recover (README and header).

wirehair_encoder_create borrows the message, which must stay allocated and unchanged until the encoder is freed, reused or detached; wirehair_encoder_create_owned copies it. Legacy decoders accept at most N + 1024 distinct packet IDs and then return Wirehair_ExtraInsufficient.

The benchmarked code is not the shipping code: the Leopard numbers came from catid/wh256, a pre-production GF256 branch now returning 404, and the encode figure appears to include the one-time encoder_create matrix solve (in the Fecal README, encode time at N = 1000 is almost the same with 99 or 31 losses: 2174 vs 2282 usec), so encode throughput is about whole-message preparation, not per-repair-packet cost.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No siblings catalogued yet. Within the author's own family, pick Wirehair over Leopard-RS when you need a rateless code or the fastest heavy-loss decode, and over Fecal when N is large or losses are heavy; pick Leopard when you need an MDS guarantee or maximum encode speed.
verified_claims_summary: Leopard's Benchmarks.md, written by the same author, reports WH256 (the GF256 pre-production branch of Wirehair) encoding 128 x 64,000-byte pieces at 661.6 MB/s and decoding at 830.1 MB/s against his CM256 Cauchy Reed-Solomon at 99.7 and 104.7 MB/s (about 6.6x and 7.9x, derived from page data), on an unnamed 'few year old' AVX2 laptop with no compiler or flags given. The run is not reproducible because the wh256 code is gone, and the decode figure is measured with about 127 of 128 originals lost, CM256's worst case.
status_note: Actively developed by its single author (frequent commits through 2026-09-17, a V2 codec, versioned ABI map and wire profiles), BSD-3-Clause and dependency-free, so copyable; but the speed claim rests on a undated first-party measurement of a deleted branch, and the repo's own current benchmarks compare only Wirehair 1 with Wirehair 2.
